title: Ordering and sets
summary: Stable sorting, multi-key ordering, Distinct and DistinctBy, the set operators and their By versions, and MinBy and MaxBy.

steps.title: Sorting is stable
body: LINQ's `OrderBy` is a **stable** sort: items with **equal keys keep their original order**. That is a promise, not luck, and it is useful.
```csharp
runners.OrderBy(r => r.Item2)    // Bo, Di, Ed, Ana, Cy
`Bo` stays before `Di` and `Ana` before `Cy`, because that is how they came in.

It also explains the "two `OrderBy`s" bug from module 6. The second sort does **not** forget the first entirely: it re-sorts everything, and only items that tie on the second key keep the first order. So `OrderBy(a).OrderBy(b)` behaves like `OrderBy(b).ThenBy(a)`, back to front. Always write `ThenBy`: it says what you mean, and it is faster.
For plain values there is `Order()` and `OrderDescending()`, no lambda needed.

steps.explain: Descending is stable too: `Ana` still comes before `Cy`. In the last line the first sort puts names Z to A; the second sort by score keeps that order inside each tie, so `Di` beats `Bo` and `Cy` beats `Ana`.

steps.title: Distinct and DistinctBy
body: `Distinct()` removes repeats, keeping the **first** of each, in the original order.
Two ways to change what "the same" means:
```csharp
// a comparer: the same email in any case
emails.Distinct(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase)
// DistinctBy: the same key means the same item
orders.DistinctBy(o => o.Customer)    // the first order of each customer
`DistinctBy` keeps the **whole first item** for each key. Combine it with sorting to keep the *best* one: sort best first, then `DistinctBy`, and the first item per key is the best.

steps.explain: Plain `Distinct` is case-sensitive, so all 5 are different. With the comparer there are 3 people. `DistinctBy` keeps the first whole email for each first letter, with its original casing: `BO@x.com`, not `bo@x.com`.

steps.title: Union, Intersect, Except
body: The set operators compare two sequences:
| Call | Gives |
| `a.Union(b)` | items in either |
| `a.Intersect(b)` | items in both |
| `a.Except(b)` | items in `a` but not in `b` |
The surprise: these are **set** operations, so the result has **no duplicates**, even if `a` had some. `a.Except(b)` is *not* the same as `a.Where(x => !b.Contains(x))`.

Each has a **By** version that compares on a key: `newStaff.ExceptBy(oldIds, s => s.Id)`. Note the second argument is a sequence of **keys**, not of items. They also take a comparer: `a.Except(b, StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase)`.
Watch `Except` drop the second `1`, even though `1` is not in the other list.

steps.explain: Set operators remove duplicates. `Where` with `Contains` keeps them. Pick the one you mean: "which customers were lost" is a set question, "which order lines are not refunds" is a filter.

steps.title: MinBy and MaxBy
body: `Max(m => m.Rating)` gives the best **rating**. Usually you want the best **movie**. Before .NET 6 people wrote `OrderByDescending(...).First()`, which sorts everything just to get one item.
```csharp
record Movie(string Title, double Rating, int Year);
double best   = movies.Max(m => m.Rating);     // 8.5
Movie  top    = movies.MaxBy(m => m.Rating)!;  // the whole movie
Movie  oldest = movies.MinBy(m => m.Year)!;
`MinBy` / `MaxBy` walk the list once. On a tie they return the **first** one. On an empty sequence of records they return `null` (hence the `!`), while `Max` throws.

steps.prompt: Match each call on `movies` to what you get back.
pairs: the first movie of each year

steps.title: Leaderboard
prompt: The tests define `record Run(string Player, int Score, int Seconds);`
Write `static List<string> Leaderboard(List<Run> runs, int top)`. Rules:
- higher `Score` is better; on equal score, fewer `Seconds` is better; still tied, `Player` A to Z
- each player appears **once**, with their **best** run
- keep the first `top` lines, numbered: `"1. Ana 900 (42s)"`
No loops. Hint: sort first, then `DistinctBy` keeps the best run per player.
starter: static List<string> Leaderboard(List<Run> runs, int top)
solution: static List<string> Leaderboard(List<Run> runs, int top)
template: {{CODE}}
var dojoRuns = new List<Run>
Dojo.Eq("top 3, best run per player", new List<string> { "1. Ana 950 (60s)", "2. Cy 900 (40s)", "3. Bo 700 (50s)" }, Leaderboard(dojoRuns, 3));
Dojo.Eq("ties broken by time then name", new List<string> { "1. Ana 950 (60s)", "2. Cy 900 (40s)", "3. Bo 700 (50s)", "4. Di 700 (50s)" }, Leaderboard(dojoRuns, 10));
Dojo.Eq("no runs", new List<string>(), Leaderboard(new List<Run>(), 3));
record Run(string Player, int Score, int Seconds);
hints: After sorting, the first run of each player is their best: `DistinctBy(r => r.Player)`.
Number the lines with `Select((r, i) => $"{i + 1}. ...")` after `Take(top)`.

steps.title: Subscribers gained and lost
prompt: Email addresses are compared **ignoring case**: `Ana@X.com` and `ana@x.com` are one person.
- `static List<string> Gained(List<string> before, List<string> now)`: emails in `now` but not in `before`, in `now`'s order, no repeats.
- `static List<string> Lost(List<string> before, List<string> now)`: emails in `before` but not in `now`, in `before`'s order, no repeats.
- `static int Loyal(List<string> before, List<string> now)`: how many people are in both.
starter: static List<string> Gained(List<string> before, List<string> now)
static List<string> Lost(List<string> before, List<string> now)
static int Loyal(List<string> before, List<string> now)
solution: static List<string> Gained(List<string> before, List<string> now)
static List<string> Lost(List<string> before, List<string> now)
static int Loyal(List<string> before, List<string> now)
template: {{CODE}}
var dojoBefore = new List<string> { "ana@x.com", "bo@x.com", "cy@x.com", "BO@x.com" };
var dojoNow = new List<string> { "Ana@X.com", "di@x.com", "ed@x.com", "DI@x.com", "cy@x.com" };
Dojo.Eq("Gained: new people, once each", new List<string> { "di@x.com", "ed@x.com" }, Gained(dojoBefore, dojoNow));
Dojo.Eq("Lost: Bo left (listed once)", new List<string> { "bo@x.com" }, Lost(dojoBefore, dojoNow));
Dojo.Eq("Loyal: Ana and Cy stayed", 2, Loyal(dojoBefore, dojoNow));
Dojo.Eq("Gained from nothing", new List<string> { "a@b.c" }, Gained(new List<string>(), new List<string> { "a@b.c", "A@B.C" }));
hints: Pass `StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase` as the last argument to compare ignoring case.

steps.title: Cheapest in each category
prompt: The tests define `record Product(string Name, string Category, decimal Price);`

Write `static List<string> Cheapest(List<Product> products)`: one line per category, sorted by category, naming its cheapest product as `"Books: Atlas (12.50)"` (price with two decimals). On a tie, the product that comes first in the list wins. Use `MinBy`, no loops.
template: {{CODE}}
var dojoProducts = new List<Product>
new("Saga", "Books", 20m), new("Mug", "Kitchen", 8m), new("Atlas", "Books", 12.5m),
new("Primer", "Books", 12.5m), new("Pan", "Kitchen", 30m), new("Kite", "Toys", 15m),
Dojo.Eq("cheapest per category, first wins a tie", new List<string> { "Books: Atlas (12.50)", "Kitchen: Mug (8.00)", "Toys: Kite (15.00)" }, Cheapest(dojoProducts));
Dojo.Eq("no products", new List<string>(), Cheapest(new List<Product>()));
record Product(string Name, string Category, decimal Price);
hints: Group by category and sort the groups by key.
Each group is a sequence of products: `g.MinBy(p => p.Price)` gives the whole product.
